title: QMaxCal: Decoherence-Aware Quantum Optimal Control via Girsanov's Theorem
claim: Regularizing with the Wiener KL term sharply collapses trajectory-level variance and stabilizes the state, unlike the baseline, drift-variance and RL policies.
layout: 4 panels in a row, shared y-axis, mean lines with shaded bands
description: A single row of four line plots with a shared y-axis for population, running from 0 to 1, and time t from 0 to 1 on each x-axis. The panels are titled Baseline (both regularizer weights 0), Wiener KL (weight 5), Drift variance (weight 5) and PPO. Each panel shows four mean population curves for the states |0> (blue), |1> (red), |+> (orange) and |Y> (green), with translucent ±1σ bands around them. Baseline curves drift smoothly and have wide bands. Wiener KL curves are nearly flat and sit near 1.0, 0.0 and 0.5 with very thin bands, and they change sharply only at the end. Drift variance curves plateau at intermediate values with moderate bands. PPO curves oscillate strongly. The eye goes first to the Wiener KL panel because its bands are narrow and its curves are flat. A legend sits in the PPO panel.
caption: SSE-trajectory population variance at $\gamma T = 2$. Mean populations across $128$ SSE samples (lines) with $\pm 1\sigma$ bands for the baseline ($\lambda_\klw=\lambda_\dvr=0$), Wiener KL ($\lambda_{\klw}=5$), drift-variance ($\lambda_{\dvr}=5$), and PPO. Wiener KL contracts the time-integrated population variance from $0.0321$ (baseline) to $0.0021$, a $15\times$ reduction, consistent with the policy routing the state along $\ker L$ where both the SSE drift and noise vanish. Drift-variance reduces the variance relative to baseline but stabilizes outside $\ker L$.
abstract: Reliable quantum control in the presence of decoherence requires policies that combat the effect of environmental noise on the controlled dynamics. Open quantum systems under continuous monitoring generate classical measurement records whose drift depends on the noise experienced by the system; the records of two evolutions sharing the same decoherence channels differ only in this drift, so Girsanov's theorem yields a closed-form, differentiable estimator of the KL divergence between their trajectory distributions. We instantiate this estimator with two physically motivated reference measures, yielding two regularizers: the Wiener KL KL W, which vanishes on the joint kernel of the Lindblad operators and is the appropriate choice when this kernel is reachable by control, and the drift-variance regularizer R DV, which, for dephasing and decay channels, vanishes if and only if the evolution is decoherence-free. Both are qualitatively distinct from existing penalties on control fluence or smoothness: they penalize the observable consequences of control on the decoherence channels rather than the control amplitude itself. The regularizers outperform unregularized gradient-based and reinforcement-learning baselines across a range of open quantum systems, including single- and multi-qubit benchmarks and a six-qubit chain calibrated to a published snapshot of the IBM Kingston processor. We evaluate them on final-state fidelity, robustness to mismatch in the assumed noise model (gains grow from +17 pp at training noise to +27 pp under 2.5 x noise mismatch), and occupation of forbidden states. The regularizers reduce infidelity by up to 50%, with ~16% gains on the calibrated IBM Kingston chain. Our code can be found at https://github.com/MerijnMoody/QMaxCal.
